That's concrete enough to set down. Here is my restatement, then how it fits the pieces we already have.

## The proposal as I understand it

- **Things:** agents, models, digital twins, typed memory objects, services and checks. They can depend on each other, and they keep changing. Your sister's company is the use case: they supply databases, their own teams build new ways to work with the data, clients add new data, and clients build new uses for it. It is one web of dependencies, with three parties changing it independently.
- **Layer 1, advertise (free):** anyone can register any thing on a Matrix server with its description, interface and dependencies. It is close to an mfuton agent skill, and to a microservice you subscribe to without handing over your file system ("type-check these functions for me").
- **Layer 2, verify (paid):** does it really do what it said it did? It is paid because verification takes work. Subscribers select with flags such as "open source only" or "doesn't touch my FS", and they have preferences among services as those services change.

## Where it sits among the R-nodes

Seen from a subscriber, this is a small AIF loop, and it maps cleanly:

| Node | In the service network |
|---|---|
| *C* | the subscriber's preferences over services (open-source only, no FS access, …) |
| R6 selection | choosing among competing services for one function |
| R7 precision | how much to trust an advertisement: advertised-only vs verified |
| R2/R3 | noticing that a service changed, and updating belief about it |
| R9 | a service's advertisement doesn't count as verification of itself |
| R17 | learning which services and verifiers turned out to be reliable |

**Change is where the value is.** A verification is a dated observation, not a permanent property. When a service updates, its verification goes stale. When an upstream dependency changes, everything downstream may go stale too. We just saw the same thing inside FUTON: the §9 census was stale three days after it was built, because the Lean changed underneath it. So the product needs more than a verification badge. It needs verification with a date, plus propagation through the dependency graph ("this check was valid against v1.3 of the thing it depends on"). For your sister's case, that propagation is the useful part: which client uses break when the schema changes.

## What can be verified, by cost

Not all "does it do what it says" questions cost the same:

1. **Licence and source:** is it open source, is the published source what actually runs? This is cheap, and existing supply-chain provenance tooling covers some of it.
2. **Effects:** doesn't touch the FS, no network access. This is moderate: sandboxed runs and static checks.
3. **Behaviour against a contract:** does the type checker actually type-check. This is expensive, and generally only partial: tests and reference cases.
4. **Exact:** where the contract is a formal statement, Lean settles it.

Tiers 1–2 are close to what registries already offer: signed publishers, provenance records, verified-publisher badges. Tier 3 is the open ground, the equivalent of the July landscape's "vacancy" records. Tier 4 is why mathematics works as the first market rather than a niche: it's the tier where "verified" means something exact.

## Business points from the earlier corpus

- **Who is obliged to pay?** The August finding was that capture depends on an obligation on the demand side. A provider paying for a badge is one option, like app-store review. A stronger one: a subscriber firm whose procurement or compliance rule says "verified services only". That rule is their *C*, written as policy, and it creates the obligation. The consulting offer and the product meet here: helping a firm write down its preference over services creates demand for verification.
- **Charge for verification from the start.** The three red cases (Docker, Lightbend, Redis) all put a price on something already adopted for free, and substitutes appeared within 1–10 days. Your framing, pay for verification because it's work and keep advertising free forever, avoids that shape. Don't later start charging for the advertise layer.
- **Avoid a single verifier.** If one party issues all verifications, it becomes the State apparatus we discussed. In a federated design, anyone can run a verifier and publish signed attestations. Subscribers choose which verifiers they trust, which is R7 applied to verifiers. Being the most careful verifier in an open field is a business; being the only one is a gatekeeper. Matrix federation already has this structure.

**The frustration measure has to separate two kinds of surprise.** The dark-room objection assumes an agent minimising surprise would sit still. AIF answers that expected free energy includes *epistemic* terms, so an agent seeks out observations that will change its model. The facade discovery was high surprisal, which you felt as dismay, followed by a large change to your model of the project. That's surprise doing its job. Repeatedly correcting an agent that doesn't take the correction on board is also surprise, but nothing gets revised. So in the stance pilot:
